Does your multifamily asset have the right amenity mix for the best results?

Elevating Multi-Family Properties

As the real estate market continues to diversify, developers, owners, and investors in multi-family properties are seeking innovative ways to enhance their portfolios and attract discerning tenants. The integration of thoughtfully chosen amenities — ranging from in-unit luxuries to expansive community features — plays a crucial role in differentiating properties in a competitive landscape, boosting return on investment (ROI), and solidifying a compelling brand image.

On behalf of a client, Brett Hunsaker and I, were asked to survey experts in the multi-family world about their take on amenities for multifamily properties.

Understanding the Demographic: The Foundation of Strategic Amenity Integration

Before delving into specific amenities, it's essential to anchor decisions in a deep understanding of the property's demographic profile. Each amenity should align with the lifestyle, expectations, and preferences of the current and target tenant base, whether they are young professionals, families, or elderly residents.

Brett Hunsaker and I reach out to contacts in the multifamily industry — developers, owners, management firms, and consultants — to understand what amenities are trending? Following are the areas of concentration in our survey.

Community Amenities: Social and Recreational Engagement

Community amenities that foster interaction and provide recreational opportunities are vital in creating a vibrant living environment.

Outdoor Amenities: Expanding Living Spaces

The design of outdoor spaces is especially critical in today’s era of remote work and increased homebound activities.

In-Unit Amenities: Enhanced Personal Living Spaces

In-unit amenities should provide comfort, convenience, and a touch of modernity, allowing for an upmarket rental positioning.

Service Amenities: Simplifying Daily Life

Consider incorporating various concierge type services to further enhance convenience for residents.

Parking and Transportation: Meeting Modern Needs

A well-thought-out parking and transportation plan is vital for convenience and accessibility.

Enhancing ROI and Brand Image Through Strategic Amenities

Investing in these amenities not only satisfies current tenant demands but also positions a property as a leader in a crowded market. This strategic approach leads to increased tenant retention, the ability to command higher rents, and an enhanced overall brand image. Properties that are seen as thought leaders in providing high-quality living experiences naturally attract more potential tenants and retain existing ones longer, thereby stabilizing income streams and reducing turnover costs.

Below is a summary list of the findings from our survey. We hope sharing the results will spark ideas to better enable you to serve, retain and amplify the resident experience. For the complete list of amenities submitted see the attachment below.

Multi-Family Amenities Summary of Survey Results 

COMMUNITY AMENITIES

Indoor Socialization Areas

Establishments like a media library, reading rooms, and diverse game rooms (featuring billiards, ping-pong, darts, and modern gaming stations) serve as central hubs for entertainment and interaction among residents.

Gourmet Kitchens and Classes

Offering indoor gourmet kitchens along with cooking classes taught by professional chefs can turn an ordinary meal prep into a community event.

Health and Wellness Facilities

Modern gyms equipped with trending fitness apparatus like Peloton bikes, yoga, and stretch classes, along with the availability of personal trainers, cater to health-conscious residents.

Specialized Rooms

A theater room for movie screenings, community wine cellars, and coffee/juice bars enhance the everyday experience by adding a touch of luxury and convenience.

Practical Additions

Features like a cyber café, a well-stocked sundry shop, and upgraded laundry rooms are not just conveniences but necessities that enrich the daily lives of tenants.

Co-Working Space

Workspace, desks, Wi-Fi, office essentials (printer, paper, pens, etc.), laptop stations, in-person and virtual meeting rooms, can offer residents the opportunity to leave their homes to avoid distractions and also a potentially long commute. 

Pet Services

Many residences enjoy pampering their pets. Services and areas such as a dog park, pet water fountain, washing stations, attendant and grooming services afford loving owners with options to keep their beloved pets healthy and happy.

OUTDOOR AMENITIES

Leisure and Cooking

Outdoor kitchens, swimming pools with a resort-like deck, and rooftop lounges extend the living space beyond the four walls of an apartment.

Active and Family Areas

Playgrounds, outdoor fitness parks, gardens for community gardening, and sports courts (including bocce ball, pickleball, and a putting green) cater to families and active adults alike.

Relaxation Zones

Fire pit areas, outdoor movie screens, and comfortable seating arrangements invite relaxation and social gatherings under the stars.

IN-UNIT AMENITIES

High-End Appliances and Fixtures

State-of-the-art kitchen appliances, designer bathrooms, smart thermostats, and in-unit laundry facilities are essential for a high-quality living experience.

Technological Enhancements

Smart locks and advanced climate control systems offer ease and efficiency, aligning with the growing demand for smart home features.

SERVICE AMENITIES

Package Delivery Solutions

A secure, tech-powered package delivery system with 24/7 access to parcels reduces hassle for both residents and staff.

Cleaning and Repair Services

On-site services like dry cleaning, shoe repair, and tech support for personal electronics ensure that residents have more time to enjoy their home environment without worrying about everyday chores.

PARKING AND TRANSPORTATION

Comprehensive Parking Solutions

Reserved spaces, ample visitor parking, designated areas for rideshare pickups, and EV charging stations.

Micro Mobility and Car Services

Facilities for bikes, scooters, and car rentals, along with regular car maintenance services, reflect an understanding of modern urban mobility.

In conclusion, by carefully selecting and integrating a range of both essential and luxury amenities tailored to the demographic and local community characteristics, multi-family property stakeholders can significantly enhance both the desirability and functionality of their offerings. This thoughtful approach ensures properties are not just seen as places to live but as homes that enrich, facilitate, and inspire a higher quality of life, thereby maximizing both ROI and tenant satisfaction.

title: Unlocking Success Through Networking in Today’s AI and Big Data World
excerpt: Are you ready to compete for new business in today’s “PUSH BUTTON” world of marketing and sales? In recent years, I have embraced AI technology. It helps me…
body:
Are you ready to compete for new business in today’s “PUSH BUTTON” world of marketing and sales?

In recent years, I have embraced AI technology. It helps me serve clients of my commercial real estate branding and marketing firm. Every day I’m amazed by the possibilities. It’s mind blowing how these technologies will continue to help us in the future.

I’ve spoken with several respected commercial real estate leaders to get their thoughts on how A.I. and Big Data will affect the commercial real estate industry and how it relates to all salespeople. I was fortunate enough to have a conversation with Brett Hunsaker, a.k.a. Mr. Shmooze, who has managed hundreds of commercial estate brokers during the last 30 years and is known for his relationship building skills.

Q: Brett, within the next few years, everybody in direct sales will be on the same playing field for contact information and social media marketing. With the advancement of AI and Big Data groups – profiling, marketing, and sales to prospects is available with a push of a button. They will be able to reach anyone but so will their competition. How can a salesperson set themselves apart from the competition?

A: Go old school! Put yourself in the best position to meet people in person and build new personal relationships.

Direct sales used to be a handshake or professionals at dinner. Today, it has become code on a server. Both are necessary in our modern world. In this ever-evolving world of business, the adage "It's not what you know, but who you know" has never been more accurate. Networking and building robust relationships are the linchpins of success in any field.

In today's digitally driven world, it's true that many salespeople are often focused on their screens rather than engaging directly with their clients. This can lead to a disconnect where salespeople are more focused on pushing their products or services rather than truly understanding and addressing the needs of their clients.

In a world where everyone has access to the same technology for contact information and social media marketing, setting yourself apart from the competition becomes crucial. While AI and Big Data tools can provide valuable insights and streamline processes, they can't replace the power of genuine human connection.

Q: You call your approach The Science of Building Relationships. Understanding and connecting with clients on a deeper level is pivotal for fostering strong and lasting relationships in business. What are the principles that can be applied in practice?

A: 1. Creating Warm Calls: Rather than reaching out to clients with a cold, purely transactional approach, aim to establish a warm connection. This could involve leveraging common interests, mutual connections, or shared experiences to initiate contact. For instance, if you both attended the same industry event or share a passion for a particular hobby, referencing these points of connection can help break the ice and make the interaction more comfortable and genuine.

2. Placing Yourself in Natural Environments: Seek out opportunities to engage with clients in settings where relationship-building can occur organically. This might involve attending industry conferences, networking events, or even social gatherings where business discussions naturally arise. By immersing yourself in these environments, you increase the likelihood of encountering potential clients in a context where rapport can develop more naturally.

3. Cultivating Meaningful Connections: Focus on building relationships that extend beyond mere transactional interactions. Take the time to get to know your clients on a personal level, understanding their goals, challenges, and preferences. Actively listen to their concerns and aspirations, and demonstrate empathy and genuine interest in their success. By investing in these deeper connections, you lay the foundation for long-term partnerships built on trust and mutual respect.

4. Fostering Genuine Relationships: Authenticity is key in building meaningful connections with clients. Avoid approaching interactions with a purely sales-oriented mindset, instead, strive to build genuine rapport based on honesty, transparency, and integrity. Be willing to share your own experiences, insights, and seek opportunities to add value to your clients' lives beyond the scope of your business transactions.

By embracing these four principles, you can elevate your relationships with clients from mere transactions to mutually beneficial partnerships founded on trust, understanding, and shared goals. This approach not only enhances client satisfaction and loyalty but also opens doors to new opportunities for growth and collaboration in the long run.

Q: Brett, how do you suggest building and elevating these relationships? 

A: Elevating touch points in relationships involves finding opportunities for in-person interactions or meaningful personal connections alongside digital interactions. The "four P's" approach can be the thought process for any communications or interactions with the target. Problem, Profit, Promotion, and Passion – can indeed be a valuable framework for enhancing these touch points:

Problem: Actively listen to clients to identify their pain points and challenges. Then, offer solutions tailored to addressing these issues. By demonstrating an understanding of their problems and providing effective solutions, you can build trust and credibility.

Profit: Look for opportunities to add value to your clients' businesses by helping them identify new revenue streams or cost-saving measures. By demonstrating how your products or services can contribute to their bottom line, you position yourself as a valuable partner rather than just a salesperson.

Promotion: Support your clients in advancing their careers or achieving their company goals. This could involve offering guidance, resources, or networking opportunities that help them excel professionally. By actively promoting their success, you strengthen your relationship and become more than just a vendor.

Passion: Connect with your clients on a personal level by understanding and aligning with their passions and interests. Whether it's through shared hobbies, philanthropic efforts, or common values, forging these personal connections can deepen the relationship and foster loyalty.

Making memorable personal touch points is crucial for standing out in a competitive market. Whether it's through creative gestures, thoughtful gestures, or memorable experiences, putting effort into creating outstanding interactions will leave a lasting impression on clients and strengthen your relationship with them.

BUILDING BLOCKS FOR EFFECTIVE NETWORKING

Q: Where do you start your process for building relationships?

A: Know Your Client — Performing a deep dive into existing clients firms and their key decision-makers can provide valuable insights and opportunities for business growth for both the existing client and target clients. Here's a structured approach to gathering relevant information:

Associations and Memberships: Identify any industry associations or professional groups that the company or key decision-makers are affiliated with. This can provide insights into their interests, industry trends, and potential networking opportunities.

Top Suppliers and Consultants: Research the primary suppliers and consultants that the company works with. Understanding these relationships can offer insights into their strategic partnerships and potential areas for collaboration.

Top Clients: Determine who the company's top clients are. This information can help you understand their customer base, industry focus, and potential referral opportunities.

Top Competitors: Identify the main competitors in the industry. Understanding the competitive landscape can help you tailor your approach and identify ways to differentiate your offerings.

Review Their Online Presence: Thoroughly review the company's website, social media platforms, and any available annual reports. Pay attention to recent news, updates, and achievements, as well as their overall messaging and brand image.

Create Cross-Selling Info Piece: Based on the gathered insights, develop a cross-selling information piece tailored to the specific needs and interests of the client. Highlight potential synergies between your products/services and their current operations, emphasizing the value proposition and benefits of collaboration.

By compiling and analyzing this information, you can better understand your clients' businesses, identify additional opportunities for engagement, and enhance your marketing and sales efforts effectively. 

Q: How can salespeople elevate their business relationships by embracing the personal touch?

A: Embracing the personal touch in business relationships is not just a nice add-on, it's essential in today's high-tech landscape. While technology enables us to connect globally at the click of a button, it's the personal, human touch that truly sets salespeople apart and strengthens relationships.

Be Genuine and Personable: Authenticity is key. Show genuine interest in your clients and colleagues. Take the time to listen to their needs, concerns, and interests. Building rapport on a personal level lays a solid foundation for fruitful business relationships.

Remember the Details: Pay attention to the little things. Remembering personal details such as birthdays, anniversaries, hobbies, and interests shows that you value the relationship beyond just the business aspect. Consider using your CRM system (most salespeople use their CRM system as a phonebook) to keep track of these details The more details that you capture will help build that relationship faster.

Thoughtful Gestures: Small acts of kindness can go a long way. Send handwritten notes expressing appreciation, congratulations, or sympathy when appropriate. Surprise your clients with thoughtful gestures like sending a personalized gift, tickets to an event they would enjoy, or arranging a lunch meeting at their favorite restaurant.

Shared Experiences: Find common ground beyond the boardroom. Discover shared interests or hobbies and leverage them to deepen connections. Organize activities or events where you can bond over mutual passions, whether it's a golf outing, attending a concert, or participating in a charity event together.

Personalized Gifts: Show your appreciation with personalized gifts that resonate with the recipient. Consider their preferences, hobbies, or aspirations when selecting gifts. For example, if a client is a sports enthusiast, signed memorabilia from their favorite team could make a memorable impression.

Celebrate Milestones: Acknowledge important milestones in your clients' lives or careers. Whether it's a promotion, a new baby, or a company anniversary, sending a congratulatory message or a small token of appreciation demonstrates that you value their partnership beyond the transactional aspect.

Maintain Regular Communication: Stay in touch with contacts regularly, not just when you have something to sell. Check in periodically through emails, phone calls or in-person meetings to see how they're doing, share relevant industry insights or resources, or simply catch up over coffee. Keep them updated on market trends, relevant news, or any opportunities that may interest them. Consistent communication helps nurture relationships over time. 

Networking Events: Attend industry-related networking events, conferences, and seminars. This provides opportunities to meet potential clients, investors, and other professionals in the field. Make sure to follow up with contacts after the event. If there’s not a networking group or association, that makes sense, I always found it beneficial to create my own networking events one that I particularly like and used often I call principal to principal mixer, bringing my clients together and creating my own business of business network.

Join Industry Associations: Become a member of relevant industry associations such as the Commercial Real Estate Development Association (NAIOP), International Council of Shopping Centers (ICSC), or local Chamber of Commerce. These organizations often host events and offer networking opportunities.

Utilize Social Media: Leverage platforms like LinkedIn to connect with prospects, share industry insights, and engage in discussions. Join industry-related groups and participate actively. Hire an expert to help you be the best in your social media program.

Volunteer Work: Get involved in community or industry-related volunteer work. This not only helps build your network but also demonstrates your commitment to giving back to the community.

Host Workshops or Seminars: Organize educational events on topics relevant to your target audience. This positions you as an expert in your field and allows you to connect with potential clients in a meaningful way.

Client Appreciation Events: Host events or dinners to show appreciation to existing clients and strengthen relationships. Encourage clients to bring along referrals or potential leads.

Referral Programs: Implement a referral program where you incentivize existing clients or contacts to refer new business to you.

Strategic Partnerships: Identify other professionals or businesses that complement your services (e.g., architects, contractors, financial advisors) and establish strategic partnerships. This can lead to referrals and collaborative opportunities.

Cold Calling/Warm Calling: While cold calling can still be effective in some cases, focus on warm calling by leveraging existing connections or referrals to initiate contact with prospects.

Personal Branding: Build your personal brand by showcasing your expertise through blogs, articles, or speaking engagements. This enhances your credibility and visibility within the industry.

CRM System: Utilize a Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system to track interactions, set reminders for follow-ups, and manage your relationships effectively.

By selecting and implementing a combination of these strategies, new salespeople can develop a comprehensive relationship plan to foster connections, build trust, and ultimately lead to business growth in the competitive commercial real estate market.

In the era of AI I wanted to see how Brett’s responses fared compared to the training ChatGPT received.

Q: How can I create better personal relationships in my sales position?

A: Prioritize In-Person Interaction: While digital communication is convenient, nothing beats face-to-face interaction when it comes to building trust and rapport. Make it a priority to attend industry events, conferences, and networking gatherings where you can meet prospects and clients in person. Take the time to engage in meaningful conversations and build genuine connections.

Focus on Personalized Service: With automation becoming more prevalent, personalized service is becoming increasingly rare and valuable. Take the time to understand each prospect's unique needs and preferences, and tailor your approach accordingly. Show genuine interest in their goals and challenges, and demonstrate how your products or services can address their specific needs.

Emphasize Relationship Building: Building strong relationships is key to long-term success in direct sales. Focus on building trust and credibility with your clients by consistently delivering value and exceeding their expectations. Keep in touch regularly, even when you're not actively selling, to maintain the relationship and stay top-of-mind.

Provide Value Beyond the Sale: Instead of focusing solely on closing the deal, focus on providing ongoing value to your clients throughout the entire sales process and beyond. Offer resources, support, and expertise that help them achieve their goals and overcome challenges. By positioning yourself as a trusted advisor rather than just a salesperson, you can build deeper, more meaningful relationships.

Differentiate Through Authenticity: In a world where everyone has access to the same technology and information, authenticity becomes a powerful differentiator. Be genuine and transparent in your interactions with clients and let your personality shine through. Authenticity builds trust and makes you more relatable, helping you stand out in a crowded marketplace.

Invest in Continuous Learning: Stay ahead of the competition by continuously learning and adapting to changes in your industry. Keep abreast of emerging trends, technologies, and best practices, and invest in professional development opportunities that help you hone your skills and stay relevant in a rapidly evolving landscape.

AI, it appears, is being trained by the best, by Mr. Shoomze himself. By prioritizing in-person interaction, personalized service, relationship building, authenticity, and continuous learning, you can set yourself apart from the competition and achieve success in direct sales, even in a world where technology levels the playing field.

CHALLENGES AND SOLUTIONS

The path to networking success isn't without its challenges. Overcoming reluctance, finding time in a busy schedule, and maintaining the sincerity of connections in a digital age are common hurdles. Solutions include setting clear networking goals, dedicating time each week to relationship-building activities, and always prioritizing quality over quantity in your connections. The goal of networking remains the same: to be the person others think of when they need a solution.

CONCLUSION

The art and science of relationship-building are more about quality than quantity. It's about making genuine connections, understanding the person behind the business card, and nurturing those relationships over time. Networking and building relationships are indispensable tools for any professional looking to thrive in today's business environment. title: What are we going to do with a million obsolete office buildings?
excerpt: Just as history has seen the reinvention of great inventions that changed our lives, the world of real estate is on the brink of a similar transformation.…
body:
Just as history has seen the reinvention of great inventions that changed our lives, the world of real estate is on the brink of a similar transformation. Consider the impact of groundbreaking inventions like the printing press, which revolutionized information dissemination, or the steam engine, which altered transportation and industry. The light bulb, telephone, aeroplane, personal computer, the Internet, and the mobile phone – each of these inventions evolved over time, significantly altering our way of life.

Today, a similar evolution is unfolding in the realm of commercial real estate. Office buildings, once symbols of corporate prowess, now face a period of obsolescence, challenging us to reimagine their role in our urban landscapes. It's time for these structures to undergo their own reinvention. The following thoughts, ideas, and concepts explore how obsolete office buildings can transform, much like the great inventions of the past, to make a meaningful impact in today's marketplace.

Housing (multi-family, senior living, affordable housing, student housing, homeless shelter) is the number one talked about conversion. It shouldn’t be the sole consideration when giving new life to an obsolete property. We asked commercial real estate (CRE) experts for other possible conversion concepts. Here is a list of innovative ideas from our respondents:

  • Medical Office
  • Life sciences / Laboratories
  • Educational facility (private schools) 
  • Self-storage
  • Recording studio
  • Media production studio 
  • Permanent filming location site
  • Training Centers / Learning center
  • Workshop
  • Dojo / Gymnasium
  • Theme / Specialty centers 
  • Youth Detention Facility
  • Cannabis / Cultivation, Retail, Testing 
  • Data Center 
  • Law enforcement / firefighter training facility
  • Library
  • Legal center

The Rise of Residential Conversions

A growing trend is the transformation of office spaces into residential units. This conversion is about creating living spaces encompassing a variety of forms such as multi-family housing, senior living facilities, student accommodations, and even affordable housing. Such conversions are particularly beneficial in urban areas, where the demand for housing often exceeds supply.

The Biden-Harris Administration introduced measures to facilitate the conversion of high-vacancy commercial properties to residential use. This includes new financing options, and technical assistance, aimed at creating affordable, energy-efficient housing. These actions are part of the White House Housing Supply Action Plan, which focuses on lowering housing costs and boosting supply.

Office vacancies averaged a 40-year high at 19.6% at the end of 2023, emphasizing the need for such initiatives. The push towards conversions is backed by the potential to add significant housing units. Research suggests that 15% of commercial district office buildings in major U.S. cities are suitable for residential conversion, potentially adding around 171,470 units.

The conversion of office spaces to residential units is often seen as a solution to revitalizing downtown areas. However, it's important to understand that while office-to-residential conversions can be beneficial in certain circumstances, they are not a panacea for all challenges faced by downtown areas. Office space utilization, despite the rise in remote work, still shows signs of recovery in certain markets. The complexity and cost of conversions often require significant public funding and support to be viable.

Specialized Spaces: Tailoring to Community Needs

Specialty conversions are gaining traction, catering to specific community needs. This includes spaces for children, seniors, fitness, healthcare, wellness, and professional services. Such specialized facilities offer a unique blend of convenience and tailored services, fostering community engagement and support.

Mixed-use developments are increasingly being recognized as more beneficial than solely residential conversions. The idea of converting office spaces to a range of uses, including coworking spaces, educational facilities, and entertainment venues, can bring more vibrancy and diversity to downtown areas. This multifaceted approach aligns with the evolving nature of work and urban life, enhancing the dynamism of city centers.

Retail Revival: Transforming Office Spaces into Marketplaces

The conversion of office buildings into retail spaces marks a significant evolution in urban land use. By transforming these areas into bustling marketplaces, cities are not only filling underused spaces but also enhancing the local shopping experience. These new retail destinations, ranging from boutiques to larger department stores, are becoming integral parts of the community fabric, offering residents and visitors alike a diverse range of shopping options. This shift is revitalizing neighborhoods, stimulating local economies, and reshaping the way we think about urban retail environments.

Medical and Wellness Centers: Fostering Health in Urban Hearts

Converting spaces into medical and wellness centers is a pivotal development in urban health infrastructure. These conversions are more than just a change in building use; they represent an investment in community health and well-being. By situating medical facilities, clinics, and wellness centers in previously vacant office buildings, cities are making healthcare services more accessible and convenient. This not only addresses critical healthcare needs but also promotes a holistic approach to wellness, integrating these vital services into the daily lives of urban dwellers.

Life Sciences and Laboratories: Pioneering New Frontiers

Dedicated spaces for life sciences and laboratories represent a groundbreaking shift in the use of former office buildings. These conversions are not just about repurposing space; they are about creating foundations for scientific breakthroughs and medical advancements. By facilitating research and development in accessible urban centers, these new labs can attract top talent, foster collaboration between academia and industry, and drive innovation in crucial fields such as biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, and environmental sciences. This trend underscores the versatility of office spaces and their potential to become key players in the global pursuit of knowledge and discovery.

Nurturing Innovation: Incubating Tech and Academic Growth

Former office buildings are now emerging as epicenters for technological innovation and academic pursuit. These spaces, once defined by corporate structure, are being creatively repurposed to nurture tech startups and educational ventures. Such environments are ideal for fostering a culture of innovation, providing budding entrepreneurs and students with the resources and space to collaborate, experiment, and drive technological progress. This shift is not just about changing physical spaces; it's about fostering a new generation of thinkers and creators, turning what were once office blocks into thriving hubs of knowledge and innovation.

Elevating Entertainment: Crafting Spaces for Joy and Engagement

The transformation of office spaces into entertainment venues opens exciting opportunities for urban areas. By converting these spaces into theaters, gaming zones, or live performance stages, cities can create new cultural focal points that attract diverse crowds and bolster the local economy. This renaissance in urban entertainment not only diversifies the cityscape but also addresses the growing demand for interactive and engaging leisure activities, contributing to the vibrancy and dynamism of city life.

Challenges and Considerations

While the potential for office space conversions is vast, it's crucial to acknowledge the complexities involved. Factors such as building regulations, structural limitations, and financial feasibility play a significant role in determining the success of these conversions. Collaborations with architects, urban planners, and financial experts are key to navigating these challenges.

The decision to convert office spaces into other uses involves several considerations, including the impact on local government revenues. It's vital to balance the need for residential spaces with the preservation of commercial property tax revenues, which are significant for many cities. This delicate balancing act is essential for maintaining fiscal stability while revitalizing urban centers.

Additionally, all new developments have a team. A team capable in that category. In conversion, the team is exponentially more important. This team needs specialists and experts with experience targeted to the conversion type. These should be experts in the fields of architecture, legal, construction, brokerage, marketing, research, capital resources. They will assure the correct planning is conducted, costs are budgeted, and issues identified before and during the conversion process. The old saying, “you need all your ducks in a row,” comes to mind, before you move forward with your concept.

The Impact on Cities and Communities

The conversion of office spaces is more than a real estate trend; it's a catalyst for urban renewal and community development. These transformations can breathe new life into declining urban areas, creating vibrant, multi-use spaces that serve a variety of community needs.

While office-to-residential conversions can contribute to solving housing shortages in urban areas, they should be viewed as part of a broader strategy. This includes incentivizing new constructions and conversions equally, ensuring that public subsidies are tied to tangible public benefits, and considering the impacts on city finances and the local economy.

Conclusion: A Future of Possibilities

The evolving landscape of office space conversions is a testament to the adaptability and resilience of the real estate sector. By reimagining these spaces, we open doors to new opportunities, meeting the changing needs of our societies and economies. As we continue to navigate this terrain, the possibilities are as limitless as our collective imagination.

title: Is Commercial Real Estate Ever Coming Back?

body:
The Past, Present, and Future of Commercial Real Estate Market Cycles

Questions we hear all the time — 

  • Will the commercial real estate market ever come back?
  • Will employees ever be back in the office?
  • How long will this last?

Believe it or not, the Commercial Real Estate (CRE) market cycle tells a optimistic story.

Just as General MacArthur said, “I shall return,” so will the CRE markets, as they have time and time again over the past decades.

The ever-evolving world of commercial real estate (CRE) is a testament to the resilience and adaptability of markets in the face of many challenges. Over the past four decades, we’ve witnessed five significant downturns in the CRE sector, each triggered by different global events. Yet, every time the dust settled, the industry rebounded stronger. Let’s review these cycles and project into the future.

A Look Back at the CRE Down Cycles

  • 1980-82: High inflation, soaring interest rates, and the repercussions of the oil embargo rattled the global economy. Add to that the overbuilding in CRE, and it’s no surprise the sector witnessed a downturn.
  • 1990-93: The Savings and Loan (S&L) crisis culminated in the creation of the Resolution Trust Corporation (RTC). Paired with the rise of telecommuting and a major stock market drop in 1989, CRE faced a challenging landscape.
  • 2001-05: The turn of the millennium was marked by the dot-com bubble burst, followed closely by the 9/11 attacks. These events saw thousands of companies vacate their office spaces, especially in lower Manhattan.
  • 2007-10: The subprime mortgage crisis hit hard. Interestingly, while telecommuting gained momentum between 2005 and 2013, many firms that embraced full remote work models began recalling employees to offices by 2014.
  • 2022-Present: Unquestionably, the Covid-19 pandemic has brought about the most profound change in recent times. The subsequent economic fallout, coupled with rising national debts, inflation, and interest rate hikes, has created an uncertain environment for CRE.

The Present State of CRE

We are currently in the throes of a downturn catalyzed by the Covid-19 pandemic. The transition to remote work, prompted by global lockdowns, has dramatically affected CRE, particularly the office sector. The present scenario is somewhat reminiscent of the telecommuting trends that emerged in the early 2010s. However, the current situation has broader implications given its global scale and the rapid technological advances supporting remote work.

On the flip side, certain segments within CRE are thriving. Warehousing and logistics centers, for instance, are seeing an uptick due to the surge in e-commerce. Similarly, data centers are proliferating with the digital transformation wave. 

Current Landscape and Projections

Next 1 Year: The pandemic’s most significant impact has been the normalization of remote work. Companies realized the viability of remote operations, leading many to reduce their physical office spaces. While this means a short-term dip in demand, the flip side is that there’s potential for CRE to diversify. Spaces can be repurposed – think co-working spaces, warehousing for e-commerce, or mixed-use developments.

Next 5 Years: The trend of urbanization isn’t going away. Cities will continue to grow, and businesses will always need commercial spaces. However, the nature of these spaces will evolve. We’ll likely see more hybrid models where offices are used for collaborations and meetings rather than daily work. Furthermore, sustainability will be at the forefront. Green buildings, efficient energy use, and other sustainable practices will not be just an added advantage but a necessity.

Next 10 Years: A decade from now, technology will play an even bigger role in CRE. Smart buildings equipped with AI, IoT, and other cutting-edge technologies will dominate the landscape. We can expect to see more flexible spaces, catering to ever-changing business needs. The CRE sector will also need to be prepared for potential challenges – be it another global crisis or the effects of climate change.

Positives Outlooks

The very nature of downturns means that there’s room for growth afterwards. With every cycle, we’ve seen innovations in the CRE sector. The rise of co-working spaces post the 2008-12 downturn is a prime example. Additionally, as technology becomes more integrated with our spaces, there’s potential for CRE to offer solutions that we haven’t even thought of yet.

Diversification of Use: The traditional usage of commercial spaces is evolving. With the rise of the digital economy, there’s a growing demand for data centers. Similarly, the healthcare sector’s expansion might increase the demand for medical office spaces.

E-Commerce and Logistics: The continued rise of e-commerce has led to a greater demand for logistics centers, warehouses, and distribution hubs, providing a significant boost to the industrial real estate segment.

Adaptive Reuse: There’s a growing trend towards repurposing old commercial spaces for new uses, like turning outdated malls into residential complexes or entertainment hubs.

Sustainable and Green Buildings: As environmental concerns rise, the demand for sustainable and green buildings is expected to grow, opening new avenues for developers and investors.

Hybrid Work Model: Although work from home has become prevalent, a hybrid model where employees work partly from home and partly from the office is gaining traction. This model still necessitates the presence of office spaces, albeit restructured for flexibility.

Challenges Ahead for CRE

External factors like global crises or economic downturns will always loom over the industry. There’s also the challenge of keeping up with rapidly changing business needs. While technology presents opportunities, it also poses threats. 

Technological Disruptions: The rapid pace of technological advancement can lead to unforeseen challenges. For instance, the rise of virtual reality could change the way retail or office spaces are conceptualized.

Remote Work: The rise of remote work can lead to reduced demand for traditional office spaces. Companies might opt for smaller offices or co-working spaces, affecting the demand dynamics of the sector.

Economic Volatility: With concerns about national debt, inflation, and interest rates, the economic environment remains uncertain. Economic downturns typically result in reduced demand for commercial spaces, at least in the short term.

Overbuilding: Historically, periods of prosperity in CRE have sometimes led to overbuilding, creating a supply-demand mismatch.

Conclusion

History has shown us that the CRE industry is adaptable and resilient. While the challenges faced in each cycle differ, the sector’s ability to adapt and innovate remains constant. As the industry navigates the post-pandemic world, it’s equipped with lessons from the past and a vision for the future.

A Commercial Real Estate Perspective

The global workforce underwent a seismic shift when the pandemic forced the majority to adapt to remote work. While the initial transition presented novel freedoms, the enduring reality has illuminated the irreplaceable advantages of the traditional office environment. From the vantage point of a commercial real estate executive, the bricks-and-mortar office isn’t just a space—it’s a breeding ground for growth, productivity, and unity.

Culture: The Heartbeat of the Corporation

The essence of a company’s culture lies in its unique environment. It’s challenging, if not impossible, to replicate the creative and stimulating milieu of an office in a remote setting. An office, adorned with brand colors and values, serves as a constant reminder of the company’s mission, inspiring employees to internalize and uphold its principles.

Collaboration and Teamwork: More Than Just Meetings

While virtual interactions offer convenience, they cannot replace the organic and spontaneous exchanges that occur within office walls. Whether it’s a serendipitous brainstorming session in the hallway or a quick lunch with a colleague, these encounters hone interpersonal skills and fortify team bonds. In essence, the physical space enhances communication, propelling not only individual but also collective performance.

Loyalty and Pride: Anchoring the Workforce

Offices play a pivotal role in cultivating loyalty. Regular face-to-face interactions reinforce bonds, making employees feel valued and less inclined to seek opportunities elsewhere. Moreover, firsthand recognition, especially from senior executives, instills pride and motivates employees to continually strive for excellence.

Relationships: The Cornerstone of Success

An office is more than just a workplace; it’s a nexus for networking. Interactions within the office and the broader building community foster both professional and personal relationships. Such relationships, difficult to cultivate virtually, are instrumental for long-term success.

Performance: Maximizing Potential

Offices enhance clarity, aligning employees with the company’s objectives. Sharing space with diverse talents spurs idea exchange, promoting innovation. Moreover, a dedicated workspace, devoid of home distractions, sharpens focus, driving productivity.

Diversity: Achieving Genuine Inclusivity

Achieving workforce diversity — a paramount goal in today’s business landscape — thrives in an in-person environment. Offices foster genuine understanding, appreciation, and collaboration across diverse groups, laying the foundation for enduring inclusivity.

Management: Streamlined and Effective

In-office management offers leaders clear channels for swift problem solving and immediate feedback, ensuring employees align with company goals. On-site presence aids hands-on training, allowing employees to directly gain from expert knowledge. The physical office environment also encourages cross-selling and streamlines recruitment, while promoting networking and mentorship among colleagues.

Work Life-Balance and Health: Delineating Boundaries

Data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics highlights a decline in productivity since Q4 of 2020, coinciding with the adoption of extended remote work. As the lines between work and home blur, the importance of a designated workspace grows. A physical office not only boosts productivity but also helps delineate work from leisure, crucial for mental health and overall productivity. Modern offices, with their emphasis on wellness programs and amenities, become bastions for holistic health, aiming for a workforce that enjoys both professional success and personal well-being.

The Tangible Impact

The decision to return to the office isn’t merely about traditionalism; It’s anchored in tangible outcomes. The structured setting of an office is conducive to enhanced productivity, a factor that invariably drives company profits. This heightened efficiency and the cohesive work environment also lead to improved retention rates, ensuring a stable and committed workforce. Additionally, an office-based operation tends to be more attractive for prospective employees, streamlining the recruitment process and drawing top-tier talent. In the larger scheme of things, the physical office isn’t just a space; It’s a strategic asset with multifaceted benefits.

Commercial Properties: Adapting for a Brighter Future

As the global business landscape evolves, so does the commercial real estate sector. Office buildings, more than ever, are prioritizing the needs and well-being of their occupants, ensuring they return to a setting that’s not only conducive to work but also nourishing for the individual.

Clean Spaces: The pandemic has underscored the importance of hygiene. Modern office buildings are now championing more rigorous cleaning protocols, ensuring every workspace is sanitized to the highest standards, instilling confidence in the occupants.

Health and Fitness: Recognizing the profound impact of physical well-being on productivity and mental health, commercial properties are now home to state-of-the-art fitness facilities. Moreover, wellness programs are frequently on offer, promoting holistic health.

Networking Opportunities: Whether for business or leisure, networking remains an integral aspect of professional growth. Many office buildings are actively curating events and platforms for both social and business networking, fostering a sense of community.

Training and Community Workspaces: Adapting to the fluid nature of modern businesses, commercial spaces now offer dedicated areas for training and community projects. These flexible zones facilitate collaboration and continuous learning.

Amenities Galore: Beyond the confines of the office, the surrounding environment plays a pivotal role in enhancing the work experience. Many commercial properties are strategically situated near or even house various amenities—be it restaurants, retail shops, or recreational zones. These conveniences further enrich the daily lives of employees.

Navigating the New Workplace Norms

In the aftermath of pandemic restrictions, several leading corporations are mandating a return to office work, reflecting a belief in the potential advantages of in-person collaboration and productivity. Giants like JP Morgan Chase, Amazon, and Salesforce have updated or abandoned earlier hybrid models in favor of more regular office attendance.* JP Morgan, for instance, expects all its managing directors to be present five days a week, and Amazon’s CEO has specified that corporate staffers be in the office for at least three days weekly. Despite these shifts, reactions from employees have varied, with some showing resistance. For example, many Amazon and Apple employees voiced their concerns, with some even resorting to petitions against the new mandates. Such directives and the ensuing responses underscore the ongoing debate on the optimal balance between remote work and office presence in the post-pandemic business landscape.

As we contemplate the future of work, it’s paramount to recognize the enduring value of the physical office. It’s not just a space — it’s an ecosystem that nurtures growth, unity, and success.
